segments.say: Lesson 17. Binary Trees: D F S & Recursion. Pre/in/post-order, "ask your children" recursion, height and diameter, and B S T validation.

Depth-first search (D F S) on a tree means going as deep as possible down one branch before backing up and trying the next, usually written with recursion. Here is an analogy. Exploring a cave system: follow one tunnel to its dead end, walk back to the last fork, and take the next tunnel.

Why does this matter? Most tree questions (height, paths, validation, diameter) are a D F S where each node combines its children's answers. A few key words. Pre-order: Visit node, then left, then right. In-order: Left, node, right (sorted order in a B S T). Post-order: Left, right, then node (children first). Subtree: A node and everything below it.

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: In-order traversal of a B S T. In-order equals left subtree, node, right subtree. On a B S T this visits values in sorted order.

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: Go left from 4, giving 2 leads to keep going left.

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: 1 has no left child leads to visit 1. Output: 1

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: Back up leads to visit 2. Output: 1, 2

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: Right subtree of 2 leads to visit 3. Output: 1, 2, 3

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: Left subtree of 4 done leads to visit 4. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4

segments.sec: Watch: In-order traversal of a BST
segments.say: Same on the right: 6, 7, 9. Final: 1,2,3,4,6,7,9, sorted. Pre-order puts the node first; post-order puts it last.

segments.sec: Watch: Recursion = ask your children (max depth)
segments.say: Recursion equals ask your children (max depth). maxDepth(node) equals 1 plus max(maxDepth(left), maxDepth(right)). Base case: an empty child returns 0.

segments.sec: Watch: Recursion = ask your children (max depth)
segments.say: The recursion dives to the leaves first. A leaf's children are empty (0), so a leaf returns 1 plus max(0,0) equals 1.

segments.sec: Watch: Recursion = ask your children (max depth)
segments.say: Parents combine their children's answers: 2 gets 2. 7 has only a right child, so it also gets 2.

segments.sec: Watch: Recursion = ask your children (max depth)
segments.say: Root: 1 plus max(2, 2) equals 3. This is the post-order pattern behind most tree problems: compute the children, then combine at the node. O of n time, O of h stack.

The recursive mindset. Base case: what do you return for None. Trust the recursion: assume f(left) and f(right) give correct answers. Combine: compute this node's answer from them. Need information flowing down (bounds, path sum so far)? Pass it as parameters. Need a global best (diameter, max path sum)? Use an outer variable updated during the post-order step.

Traversal orders. Pre-order (node, L, R): copy or serialize a tree, root-to-leaf paths. In-order (L, node, R): B S T in sorted order, k-th smallest. Post-order (L, R, node): heights, diameters, deleting a tree. Children first.

Gotchas. B S T validation must check bounds from ancestors, not just the parent. Recursion depth: a skewed tree with 10 to the 5 nodes can exceed Python's recursion limit. Mention an iterative stack alternative. Space is O of h: O of log n when balanced, O of n when skewed.

segments.sec: Problem 1: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
segments.say: Problem 1: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree. Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. For example, with 3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7, the answer is 3. 3, giving 20, giving 15

segments.sec: Problem 1: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
segments.say: The obvious brute force: List every root-to-leaf path and take the longest. Wasteful bookkeeping. That costs O of n time but clunky. The smart way: Post-order: 1 plus max of the children's depths. Step by step: Empty tree, giving 0. Then, Depth equals 1 plus max(depth of left, depth of right).
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of h space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 2: Validate Binary Search Tree. Check whether a binary tree is a valid B S T: every node's left subtree holds only smaller values and its right subtree only larger values. For example, with 2, 1, 3, the answer is True.
What is it really asking? The trap is checking only each node against its parent. A node deep down must respect every ancestor's limit.

The obvious brute force: In-order traversal into a list, then check the list is strictly increasing. That costs O of n time, O of n memory. The smart way: Pass down an allowed (lo, hi) range: going left tightens hi, going right tightens lo. Step by step: Recurse with an allowed range (lo, hi), starting at ( minus ∞, +∞). Then, The node's value must be strictly inside the range. Then, Going left, the max becomes node.val; going right, the min becomes node.val.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of h space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 3: Diameter of Binary Tree. Return the length (in edges) of the longest path between any two nodes of a binary tree. The path doesn't have to pass through the root. For example, with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the answer is 3. 4, giving 2, giving 1, giving 3 (or 5, giving 2, giving 1, giving 3)

The obvious brute force: For every node, compute left height plus right height separately (each height call is O of n ). That costs O of n squared time. The smart way: At each node the longest path through it equals left height plus right height. Return height upward and track the global best. Step by step: Write height(node) recursively. Then, Inside it, the longest path bending through this node equals left height plus right height, so update a global best. Then, Return 1 plus max(left, right) as the height.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of h space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: How do you approach any binary tree problem? A strong answer: Decide what each call returns for a subtree, define the None base case, trust the recursive calls on the children, and combine. If the answer can pass through a node (diameter, max path sum), keep a global best updated in post-order.
